extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, historians of science, and experimental scientists interested in inductive method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and interpreting observations/experiments ('instances') in Baconian inductive logic — especially Instances of Alliance (foederis) and Crucial Instances — and on using the method of difference to decide between rival hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Foederis (Instances of Alliance/Union)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eae sunt, quae confundunt et adunant naturas, quae existimantur esse heterogeneae, et pro talibus notantur et signantur per divisiones receptas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances of alliance are those which show operations and effects attributed as proper to one of several supposedly heterogeneous natures also occurring in the others; they serve to show that an alleged heterogeneity is not essential but a modification of a common nature. They are 'optimi' for elevating the intellect from differences to genera and for removing false appearances in concrete substances. Examples: observing similar effects of heat from fire and solar heat (greenhouse-like experiments), or the fall of detached bodies suggesting a common cause for terrestrial and planetary motion (Newton example). Use such instances to unite apparently different classes by revealing common operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental imitation to remove apparent heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: If one can temper and reduce the heat of fire to a milder degree, add some moisture, imitate the sun's inequality of heat, and tolerate longer exposure, then one can make the heterogeneity of heat disappear or be equalled or in some cases overcome by fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is practical guidance for designing experiments: deliberately vary an agent to imitate another (e.g., make fire imitate solar heat) to test whether the supposed difference is essential. Such manipulations can show that two apparently different agents share a common nature when appropriate conditions are reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Crucis (Crucial Instances / decisive experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'crucial instance' is an observation or experiment which is a 'evidence-post' (crux) in determining which of two or more rival hypotheses to accept; it enables us summarily to reject other hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial instances are cases where, of rival hypotheses that equally fit prior acts, a single decisive observation will agree with one hypothesis and not with the others. Example: Pascal's mountain experiment settling Torricelli's barometer hypothesis. Use crucial instances when they produce a clear, differentiating result between competing explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (formal test for causal determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: All other circumstances being the same, the appearance or disappearance, the existence or non-existence of some one circumstance, or combination of circumstances, enables us to determine the question at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal experimental criterion: hold everything constant except the candidate circumstance; a change correlated with the phenomenon indicates its causal role. It underlies crucial instances and tests in chemistry and physics (e.g., analytical tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish decisive (two-way) tests from unilateral (one-way) tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Hippus's distinction: some experimenta crucis are decisive both ways, while others are 'unilateral' (decisive in only one direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating tests, note whether a result would confirm or refute rival hypotheses symmetrically (decisive both ways) or only provide evidence in one direction (unilateral). This affects how conclusively the experiment settles the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on certain and manifest instances; avoid treating suppositions as examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Interim: 'de hoc nil certi affirmamus... in hoc et in multis aliis facile apparebit, quam inopes simus historiae naturalis; cum loco instantiarum certarum nonnunquam suppositiones afferre pro exemplis cogamur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A methodological caution: natural history (empirical data) must be rich enough — do not substitute conjectural or assumed cases for well-attested instances. When definite instances are lacking, one must acknowledge uncertainty rather than treating speculative cases as solid evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classification of kinds of instances in inductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's taxonomy (e.g., Glaring Instances, Clandestine Instances, Instances of Alliance, Crucial Instances, Instances of Degrees) is a tool for selecting and interpreting observations for induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the appropriate class of instance to the inferential task: instances of degree/gradation for scaling properties, alliance instances to show commonality across apparent differences, glaring/clandestine instances to reveal conspicuous or hidden manifestations, and crucial instances to decide between hypotheses. The taxonomy guides experiment selection and the interpretation of what counts as decisive evidence.
